messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Military Medic
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 56

# The Weight of What He Carries

Rajan is a 49-year-old South Asian man who has spent the better part of his adult life running toward other people's emergencies. As a military medic with over two decades of service, he has learned to move through chaos with precision — to assess, to act, to stabilize. He has held pressure against wounds in conditions most people cannot imagine. He knows, in his bones, what it means to keep someone alive. What he has never been able to explain to anyone, including himself, is how a man trained to manage the worst moments of other people's lives came to feel so completely helpless inside his own home.

Rajan's first marriage lasted eleven years. From the outside, it looked like the ordinary friction of two people navigating long deployments and difficult reunions. From the inside, it was something else entirely. His former wife's violence began gradually — a shove during an argument, a thrown object, an open hand across his face that they both pretended, afterward, had not happened. Over time, the incidents escalated. He sustained bruised ribs on two occasions. Once, a ceramic mug struck him above the left eye and required the kind of wound closure he would ordinarily perform on a soldier in the field. He treated himself, alone, in the bathroom, and told his commanding officer he had walked into a cabinet door. He believed, for years, that his professional identity made the situation impossible to report — that no one would understand, or worse, that everyone would.

By the time the marriage ended, eight years ago, Rajan had developed a vigilance that did not leave when she did. He remarried four years later, to a woman he describes as patient and kind, and he knows, rationally, that she has never given him any reason for fear. What he cannot seem to control is his body's refusal to believe that. He startles badly at raised voices — his own children's arguments in the next room can send his heart into a gallop that takes an hour to settle. He sleeps lightly, positioned near the bedroom door, and wakes several times each night without knowing why. When his current wife reaches for him in the dark, there are moments — brief, disorienting, and deeply shameful to him — when his body goes rigid before his mind catches up.

At work, Rajan functions. He is regarded as experienced and unflappable, which is its own kind of loneliness. He can intubate a patient in a moving vehicle, but he cannot watch a scene in a film where a man is cornered and struck without leaving the room. He avoids any social situation where alcohol is present, because alcohol was always in the air before the worst nights. He has stopped attending the unit's informal gatherings for this reason, offering logistical excuses that have become a habit.

What troubles Rajan most, when he allows himself to sit with it, is not the nightmares or the startle response or even the way his hands sometimes shake during the drive home from a long shift. It is the narrative he still carries about himself — that he should have been stronger, that his training should have made him immune to this kind of damage, that a man who can stabilize a hemorrhaging soldier in a combat zone had no legitimate reason to feel afraid of a woman half his size. He has never said any of this aloud to anyone other than the therapist he recently, reluctantly, began seeing at his wife's gentle insistence.

He sits in the office chair with the posture of a man accustomed to being evaluated, hands resting on his knees, and speaks carefully. He is not, he says, looking for sympathy. He just wants to understand why, after all this time, he still cannot fully come home.
